To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
estrogen induces synthesis of a specific cytosol protein of 45kDa, but not of total cellular proteins, nuclear proteins, or estrogen receptor in the aging uterus of rats.
the uterine responsiveness of old rats to estrogen is impaired.

aging is associated with a decrease in the synthesis of estrogen receptor, total cellular, and acid-soluble proteins, and that this decreased synthesis of proteins is further reduced by the administration of estrogen.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of aging on the uterotropic action of estrogen.
the study of the molecular basis of estrogen action in young and old rats.
the age-related decline of estrogen-induced protein synthesis in rat uterus.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
estrogen-induced protein synthesis declines with age.
the uterine response to estrogen declines during aging.
the estrogen receptor is present in the old rat uterus but the synthesis of the estrogen receptor protein as well as the other uterine proteins is significantly lower.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the estrogen-induced synthesis of proteins is reduced in old age.
the estrogen receptor and the estrogen responsive genes are downregulated in the uterus during aging.

the synthesis of estrogen receptor, estrogen-inducible proteins and the specific protein of 45kDa are significantly decreased in old compared to young rats and this decline is due to the reduced responsiveness of the uterus to the estrogenic stimulation in old age.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the decline in the estrogen-induced synthesis of uterin proteins during aging may be due to the decline in estrogen receptors and/or the reduced transcriptional activity of estrogen response elements.
estrogen-induced synthesis of proteins declines during aging and that the synthesis of a 45 kDa protein is specifically affected.
the synthesis of a 45 kDa protein is estrogen-dependent in young but not old rats.
